record.paper_title: Open problems in ageing science: A roadmap for biogerontology
record.original_question: How much do positive feedback loops and chain reactions contribute to ageing?

evidence.quote: How much do positive feedback loops and chain reactions contribute to ageing?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Consider an organism modelled as a dynamical network of interacting molecular, cellular, and physiological components, in which damage accumulates over time and gives rise to the phenotype called ageing (the time-dependent decline in functional capacity and increase in mortality risk). A "positive feedback loop" in this network is a directed cycle of causal influences whose net gain is positive, so that an increase in damage or dysfunction at one node eventually produces a further increase at the same node. A "chain reaction" is a (not necessarily cyclic) cascade in which damage at one node propagates to and amplifies damage at downstream nodes. Quantify the contribution of such positive feedback loops and damage-propagating chain reactions to the overall ageing process: specifically, determine what fraction of the age-related increase in damage, dysfunction, and mortality across the lifespan is attributable to self-reinforcing feedback and cascading amplification, as opposed to independent, additive accumulation of primary damage events.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of how much positive feedback loops and damage cascades contribute to ageing remains an open conceptual and quantitative problem in biogerontology. While vicious-cycle hypotheses (e.g. mitochondrial-ROS feedback, senescence-induced senescence/SASP, inflammageing) are widely discussed in the literature, no consensus quantitative attribution exists.

status_evidence.snippet: Lists feedback loops in ageing among unresolved open problems.
status_evidence.claim: The contribution of positive feedback loops and chain reactions to ageing is identified as an unresolved open question.
